skills.title: Explain what a scientific model is and why it leaves out details on purpose
Decide which details matter and which can be ignored for a given question
Recognise that the branches of science share ideas, tools and models

expectations: A model is a simplified representation (a picture, an equation, an object or an idea) that keeps only the features needed to answer a particular question.
Leaving out details is deliberate, not a mistake: it makes the problem solvable and the main pattern visible.
Which details can be ignored depends on the question; a detail that is safe to ignore for one question may be essential for another.
A good model is judged by whether its predictions match observations; when they do not, the model is refined.
Physics, chemistry, biology and earth science overlap: the same ideas (energy, particles, models) are used across them.

misconceptions.belief: A model is wrong or useless because it leaves out details of the real thing.
signs: Says 'a cricket ball is not a point, so the model is wrong'
Rejects a map because it does not show every tree
Wants every detail included before using a model

skills.title: Write physical quantities as number plus SI unit and use standard symbols
Convert between common units (g-kg, cm-m, min-s, km/h-m/s)
Explain why standard units and consistent units in equations matter

expectations: A measured quantity has a number and a unit; the number alone is meaningless.
SI base units used here: metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, kelvin (K) for temperature; derived units like m/s and N come from them.
Before putting values into an equation, all quantities must be in consistent units.
Standard units let people anywhere compare and trust measurements; mixed units have caused real accidents.
Symbols (like v for speed, m for mass) make relationships short and exact, and each symbol has a defined meaning and unit.

misconceptions.belief: Once you have the number, the unit is optional.
signs: Writes 'answer = 25' without a unit
Adds 2 m and 30 cm to get 32
Thinks 500 and 500 g say the same thing

skills.title: Distinguish observation, hypothesis, law and theory
Explain the scientific meaning of 'theory' versus the everyday meaning
Explain how evidence can support or overturn scientific ideas

expectations: A hypothesis is a testable, tentative explanation or prediction that experiments can support or reject.
A law describes a pattern that always holds under stated conditions, often as a short statement or equation (what happens).
A theory is a well-tested, evidence-backed explanation that ties many observations and laws together (why it happens); it is not a guess.
In everyday talk 'theory' means a hunch; in science it is the strongest kind of explanation.
Scientific ideas are trusted because they survive many tests, yet they can be revised if strong new evidence disagrees.

misconceptions.belief: A scientific theory is just a guess or an unproven idea.
signs: Says 'it's only a theory'
Ranks theory below a hypothesis
Thinks theories become laws when proved

expectations: The cell membrane is selectively permeable: it lets some substances through and controls what enters and leaves.

Cytoplasm holds organelles: mitochondria release energy from food (respiration), ribosomes make proteins, ER and Golgi make and package materials, lysosomes break down waste.

Cells are three-dimensional; a diagram or slide shows a thin flat slice.

skills.title: Explain why organisms grow by making more cells rather than bigger cells
Describe mitosis: one cell gives two identical cells, used for growth and repair
Describe meiosis: gives cells with half the chromosomes, used to make gametes and variation

expectations: Living things grow and repair mainly by increasing the number of cells through cell division, not by cells growing endlessly.
A cell cannot grow very large because its surface (membrane) would be too small to supply its volume; dividing keeps cells small.
Mitosis makes two daughter cells with the same number and type of chromosomes as the parent; it is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
Meiosis happens in reproductive organs and makes four cells with half the chromosomes; these gametes join at fertilisation to restore the full number.
Meiosis shuffles chromosomes, so gametes differ and offspring show variation.

skills.title: State the three ideas of the cell theory
Trace how microscopes and evidence built the cell theory (Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow)
Use the cell theory to reason that cells come only from existing cells

expectations: All living things are made of one or more cells.
The cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life.
All cells come from pre-existing cells by division.
Hooke saw empty box-like cell walls in cork (1665); Leeuwenhoek saw living single cells; Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) generalised; Virchow added that cells come from cells.

skills.title: Distinguish meristematic (dividing) tissue from permanent tissue
Locate apical, lateral and intercalary meristems and link each to a kind of growth

expectations: Plant growth happens only in certain regions that have meristematic tissue, whose cells keep dividing.

Apical meristem at root and shoot tips makes the plant longer; lateral meristem (cambium) makes stems and roots thicker; intercalary meristem at the base of leaves or internodes (as in grasses) lets those parts grow back.
Meristem cells are small, thin-walled, packed with dense cytoplasm and a big nucleus, with few or no vacuoles.

Permanent tissues are cells that have stopped dividing and taken up a specific job: parenchyma (storage, packing), collenchyma (flexible support), sclerenchyma (hard, dead, strength, e.g. coconut husk), epidermis (protection).
Xylem carries water and minerals up from roots; phloem carries food made in leaves to other parts.

skills.title: Name the four types of animal tissue and a job of each

expectations: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together for a function.
Epithelial tissue covers and lines surfaces (skin, inner lining of mouth and gut), protecting and controlling exchange.
Connective tissue joins and supports: bone, cartilage, ligaments (bone to bone), tendons (muscle to bone), fat, and blood (cells in a fluid matrix, plasma).
Muscular tissue contracts to cause movement: skeletal (voluntary), smooth (involuntary, in gut walls), cardiac (heart, never tires).
Nervous tissue (neurons) carries messages as electrical signals quickly over long distances.
A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament; ligaments have a poor blood supply, so they heal slowly.

skills.title: Explain that muscles only pull (contract) and work in antagonistic pairs

expectations: Muscles can only contract (shorten) and pull; they cannot push.
So muscles work in pairs: when one contracts the other relaxes (e.g. biceps bends the elbow, triceps straightens it).
Muscles are attached to bones by tendons; bones meet at joints held by ligaments, with cartilage reducing friction.

Ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip) allow movement in all directions and rotation; hinge joints (elbow, knee) allow back-and-forth in one plane; pivot joint (between first two neck vertebrae) allows turning the head.
Bones are levers and joints are pivots; muscles supply the pulling force.

expectations: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time; unit m/s.
Velocity is speed in a given direction; average velocity = displacement ÷ time; it can be zero even when speed is not.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = (v − u)/t, unit m/s².
Acceleration includes slowing down (negative acceleration, deceleration) and changing direction, not just speeding up.
An object can have zero velocity for an instant and still be accelerating, e.g. a ball at the top of its throw, where gravity still changes its velocity at about 9.8 m/s² downward.

expectations: A solution is a homogeneous mixture: the solute is spread evenly through the solvent as particles too small to see or settle.
Concentration tells how much solute is in a given amount of solution, e.g. mass % = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100.
Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a fixed amount of solvent (often 100 g water) at a given temperature.
A saturated solution holds the maximum solute at that temperature; a concentrated solution simply has a lot of solute, saturated or not.
For most solids, solubility rises with temperature, so a hot saturated solution forms crystals on cooling.
Dissolving is not melting: the solute's particles spread between solvent particles at room temperature; mass is conserved.

skills.title: Choose a separation method from the properties of the components
Explain crystallisation, evaporation, sublimation, separating funnel and chromatography
Compare methods for purity and suitability

expectations: Separation methods use a difference in a property: particle size, solubility, boiling point, density, ability to sublime, or how far a substance travels with a solvent.
Evaporation removes the solvent but leaves all dissolved impurities with the solid; crystallisation gives purer crystals because impurities stay dissolved in the leftover liquid.
A separating funnel separates two immiscible liquids (oil and water) by density: the denser layer is drained from the bottom.
Sublimation separates a solid that changes directly to vapour (camphor, ammonium chloride, naphthalene) from one that does not (salt).
Chromatography separates coloured components that dissolve in a solvent and travel at different rates on paper (e.g. dyes in ink).
Distillation separates a liquid from dissolved solids or two miscible liquids with different boiling points.

skills.title: Classify mixtures as solutions, colloids or suspensions by particle size and behaviour
Explain the Tyndall effect and use it as a test
Name everyday colloids and their dispersed phase and medium

expectations: Solutions have tiny particles (below about 1 nm), are transparent, do not settle and pass through filter paper.
Suspensions have large particles (often visible to the eye), look cloudy, settle on standing and can be filtered.
Colloids have intermediate particles; they look uniform, do not settle easily, pass through filter paper and scatter light.
The Tyndall effect is the scattering of a light beam by colloid or suspension particles, making the beam visible; true solutions do not show it.
Milk, fog, butter, smoke, jelly and shaving foam are colloids: a dispersed phase spread in a dispersion medium.

skills.title: Find the net force from forces acting along one line
Relate balanced forces to no change in motion and unbalanced forces to a change
Explain friction as a force opposing relative motion and its everyday roles

expectations: The net force is the combined effect of all forces on an object; forces in the same direction add, in opposite directions subtract.
Balanced forces (net force zero) do not change motion: an object at rest stays at rest; a moving object keeps moving at constant velocity.
Unbalanced forces (net force not zero) change the speed or direction of motion.
A moving object slows down on its own because friction (and air resistance) act against motion, not because it 'runs out of force'.

expectations: First law: an object stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless an unbalanced force acts on it.
Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist a change in its motion; more mass means more inertia.
Second law: the net force equals the rate of change of momentum; for constant mass, F = ma. 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
Momentum p = mv; a larger force or a longer time changes momentum more.
A force is not stored in or used up by a moving object; motion continues without force unless friction or another force changes it.
Without air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s², because a heavier object has proportionally more inertia.

skills.title: State the conditions for work in physics: a force and a displacement along the force

expectations: In physics, work is done only when a force acts on an object and the object is displaced in the direction of the force (or has a component along it).
W = F × s when force and displacement are along the same line; unit joule (J) = 1 N × 1 m.

Work is positive when force and displacement are in the same direction (lifting a bag up), negative when opposite (friction on a sliding box), zero when the displacement is zero or perpendicular to the force.
Holding a heavy bag still, or carrying it horizontally at constant height, does no work on the bag against gravity, even though you feel tired (your muscles use energy internally).
Everyday 'work' (effort, a job) is not the same as physics work.

skills.title: Calculate kinetic energy KE = ½mv²
Calculate gravitational potential energy PE = mgh
Apply conservation of mechanical energy (KE + PE constant without friction)
Explain that energy is transformed, not used up, and track where 'lost' energy goes

expectations: Kinetic energy is energy of motion: KE = ½mv²; doubling speed makes it four times bigger.
Gravitational potential energy is energy due to height: PE = mgh, measured from a chosen reference level.
Without friction or air resistance, KE + PE stays constant: as an object falls PE turns into KE and vice versa.
On a swing, PE is greatest and KE least at the highest points; KE is greatest at the lowest point.
Energy is never destroyed: when a swing slows down, mechanical energy changes to heat and sound through friction and air resistance; total energy is conserved.

signs: Says a swing stops because its energy finished

Cannot say where the energy went

skills.title: Identify levers (three classes), pulleys and inclined planes in daily life
Explain mechanical advantage: a machine trades force for distance
Explain why no machine reduces the work done (it can only make it easier)

expectations: A simple machine changes the size or direction of a force to make a task easier.
Mechanical advantage (MA) = load ÷ effort; MA greater than 1 means less effort is needed.
Less effort always comes with moving the effort through a larger distance: work in ≥ work out.
A machine never reduces the work needed; at best (no friction) work in equals work out; with friction more work is needed.

A single fixed pulley (as at a well) gives MA about 1 but changes the direction of the force, letting you pull down to lift up; an inclined plane (ramp) lets you push with less force over a longer distance.
Lever classes depend on the position of fulcrum, load and effort: class 1 (seesaw, scissors), class 2 (nutcracker, wheelbarrow), class 3 (tweezers, forearm).

workedExample.problem: A 3 m ramp is used to push a 600 N crate onto a 1 m high platform with a 250 N push. Find the ideal force, the actual work and the extra work against friction.
steps: Useful work = load × height = 600 × 1 = 600 J
Ideal (frictionless) force = 600 J ÷ 3 m = 200 N
Actual work by the pusher = 250 × 3 = 750 J
Extra work against friction = 750 − 600 = 150 J
MA (actual) = 600/250 = 2.4; the ramp eased the force but did not reduce the work

skills.title: Trace the idea of atoms from Kanada's parmanu to Dalton
Describe Thomson's, Rutherford's and Bohr's models and the evidence for each
Explain the limits of each model and why models changed

expectations: Maharshi Kanada (ancient India) proposed indivisible particles called parmanu; Dalton (1808) made atoms a scientific theory with evidence from the laws of chemical combination.
Thomson discovered the electron and proposed a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded (like seeds in a watermelon).
Rutherford's gold foil experiment: most alpha particles passed straight through, a few were deflected, very few bounced back; so an atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
Bohr proposed that electrons move only in certain allowed energy levels (shells) without losing energy, fixing the instability problem in Rutherford's model.
Atoms are far too small to see with an ordinary light microscope; we know about them from indirect evidence, and modern instruments only image their positions.
Electron 'orbits' are a model; electrons do not move like planets on fixed paths.

expectations: Protons (+1 charge, mass about 1 u) and neutrons (no charge, about 1 u) are in the nucleus; electrons (−1 charge, about 1/1840 u) are outside.

Mass number A = protons + neutrons (nucleons); electrons are not counted because their mass is tiny.

skills.title: Write electron distributions (K, L, M, N) for the first 20 elements using 2, 8, 8 filling

expectations: Electrons fill shells from the innermost: K holds up to 2, L up to 8; for the first 20 elements M is filled to 8 before N starts (e.g. K = 2, 8, 8, 1; Ca = 2, 8, 8, 2).
The outermost shell's electrons are the valence electrons.
Atoms tend to reach a stable full outer shell (8, or 2 for the K shell alone) by losing, gaining or sharing electrons.
Valency = number of electrons lost, gained or shared to reach a full shell: it equals the valence electrons if 1-4, and 8 minus valence electrons if 4-8.
Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar) already have full outer shells, so their valency is 0 and they hardly react; neon signs glow because electricity excites electrons, not because neon reacts.

skills.title: Define isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons

expectations: Isotopes are atoms with the same atomic number (same protons, same element) but different mass numbers (different neutrons).
Examples: hydrogen-1, hydrogen-2 (deuterium), hydrogen-3 (tritium); carbon-12 and carbon-14; chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.
Isotopes have nearly identical chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons; physical properties like mass and density differ.

Some isotopes are radioactive (unstable nuclei); uses include cobalt-60 in cancer treatment, iodine-131 for thyroid disorders, uranium-235 in nuclear reactors, carbon-14 for dating old organic remains.
Isobars are different: different elements with the same mass number.

skills.title: State the law of conservation of mass and apply it to reactions in closed and open containers
State the law of constant proportions and use mass ratios
Explain how these laws supported Dalton's atomic theory

expectations: Law of conservation of mass: in a chemical reaction mass is neither created nor destroyed; total mass of reactants = total mass of products.
An apparent loss or gain of mass in an open container means a gas escaped or was taken in from the air; in a sealed container the mass stays the same.
When something burns, its atoms combine with oxygen to form products, many of them gases (carbon dioxide, water vapour) that escape; the mass is not lost, it moves into the air.
Law of constant proportions: a pure compound always contains the same elements in the same fixed ratio by mass (water is always 1 : 8 hydrogen to oxygen by mass), however it is made.
Dalton explained both laws: atoms are not created or destroyed in reactions, they only rearrange, and each compound has a fixed ratio of atoms with fixed masses.

expectations: Ionic bonds form when a metal atom transfers electrons to a non-metal atom; the resulting positive and negative ions attract strongly (e.g. Na⁺Cl⁻).
Covalent bonds form when non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons so each gets a full outer shell (e.g. H₂, H₂O, CH₄).
Ionic compounds: usually solids with high melting points, often soluble in water, and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved because their ions can move.
Solid ionic compounds do not conduct, because their ions are locked in place in the crystal.
Covalent compounds like sugar: generally lower melting points, and do not conduct electricity even in solution because they form no free ions.

expectations: A chemical formula shows the elements in a compound and the number of atoms of each.
To write a formula, write the symbols (positive part first), write valencies, criss-cross them as subscripts, and simplify to the lowest ratio (e.g. Al³⁺ and O²⁻ → Al₂O₃).
Polyatomic ions such as OH⁻, CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻, NH₄⁺ are treated as single units; brackets are used when more than one is needed, e.g. Mg(OH)₂.
Charges must balance: the total positive charge equals the total negative charge, which is why NaCl, not NaCl₂.
Molecular mass (for molecules) or formula unit mass (for ionic compounds) = sum of atomic masses of all atoms in the formula, in u.

skills.title: Explain that sound is produced by vibrating objects

Describe sound as a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions in which particles vibrate in place

expectations: Every sound comes from something vibrating: a tabla skin, vocal cords, a guitar string, a speaker cone.
Sound needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel; it cannot travel through a vacuum, which is why astronauts on the Moon use radios.
Sound in air is a longitudinal wave: particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel, forming compressions (crowded) and rarefactions (spread out).

Light can travel through a vacuum, which is why we see the Sun but cannot hear it.

skills.title: Relate frequency to pitch and amplitude to loudness
Use v = f × λ to calculate speed, frequency or wavelength
Compare the speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases, and state the human hearing range

expectations: Frequency is the number of vibrations per second (hertz, Hz); higher frequency = higher pitch.
Amplitude is the size of the vibration; larger amplitude = louder sound. Pitch and loudness are independent.
Wavelength λ is the distance between two consecutive compressions; speed v = f × λ.
Sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases (air ~343 m/s at 20 °C, water ~1500 m/s, steel ~5000-6000 m/s); in air it is faster at higher temperature.
Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz; below is infrasound (elephants, earthquakes), above is ultrasound (bats, dolphins).
Thinner, tighter, shorter strings vibrate at higher frequencies: the veena's thin strings give high notes, thick strings low notes.

skills.title: Explain reflection of sound and when a distinct echo is heard
Calculate distance from echo time using d = v × t / 2
Explain reverberation and how halls reduce it
Explain uses of ultrasound and echolocation (SONAR, bats, medical scans)

expectations: Sound reflects from hard surfaces, obeying the same laws as light (angle of incidence = angle of reflection).
An echo is heard as separate only if it arrives at least about 0.1 s after the original sound; at ~344 m/s the reflecting surface must be at least about 17 m away.
Echo distance: the sound travels to the wall and back, so distance = speed × time ÷ 2.
Reverberation is the persistence of sound from many quick reflections in a hall; soft materials (curtains, carpets, cushioned seats, acoustic panels) absorb sound and reduce it.
Bats and dolphins use echolocation; ships use SONAR to measure sea depth; doctors use ultrasound scans because ultrasound reflects from tissue boundaries.
Domes like the Gol Gumbaz in Bijapur focus reflected sound so a whisper can be heard across the gallery.

expectations: Asexual reproduction needs only one parent and no gametes; offspring are produced by mitosis.
Modes: binary fission (Amoeba, bacteria), budding (yeast, Hydra), fragmentation (Spirogyra), spore formation (bread mould), regeneration (Planaria).
Vegetative propagation grows new plants from roots, stems or leaves: potato eyes (stem tubers), sugarcane stem pieces, Bryophyllum leaf buds, rose cuttings, mango grafting.
Offspring are genetically identical to the parent (clones), so desirable traits like sweet mangoes or disease-free sugarcane are kept exactly.
Lack of variation is a risk: one disease can wipe out a whole crop of identical plants.

skills.title: Identify flower parts (sepal, petal, stamen, pistil) and their roles
Explain pollination (self and cross) and agents such as insects and wind
Describe fertilisation and seed and fruit formation
Explain how meiosis and fertilisation create variation

expectations: The stamen (anther and filament) makes pollen grains containing male gametes; the pistil (stigma, style, ovary) contains ovules with female gametes.
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma; self-pollination is within the same flower or plant, cross-pollination between plants, by insects, birds, wind or water.
After pollination a pollen tube grows down the style to an ovule, where a male gamete fuses with the egg (fertilisation) to form a zygote.
The zygote develops into an embryo inside the seed; the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary ripens into the fruit.
Gametes are made by meiosis and each carries a different mix of genes; fertilisation combines two parents' genes, so offspring vary.
Without pollination and fertilisation most flowers do not form fruit or seeds (a few plants form fruit without it, e.g. some banana varieties).

skills.title: Describe changes at puberty and why they happen (hormones), and that the timing varies
Name the main human reproductive organs and their roles in outline
Outline fertilisation and pregnancy (zygote, embryo, placenta) in simple terms
Explain reproductive health: hygiene, nutrition, consent and body safety, and where to get trusted help

expectations: Puberty is the stage when the body becomes capable of reproduction, triggered by hormones (testosterone, oestrogen); it usually begins between about 8-14 years and the timing varies from person to person.
Common changes: growth spurts, body hair, voice changes, acne, breast development and menstruation in girls, broader shoulders and facial hair in boys, plus emotional changes.

Male organs: testes make sperm and testosterone; sperm travel through the sperm ducts. Female organs: ovaries release an egg about once a month and make oestrogen; oviducts carry the egg; the uterus is where a baby develops.

Fertilisation of the egg by a sperm usually happens in the oviduct; the zygote divides and the embryo implants in the uterus wall; the placenta supplies food and oxygen and removes waste; pregnancy lasts about nine months.
Menstruation is a normal monthly shedding of the uterus lining when no fertilisation occurs; hygiene and nutrition (iron, protein) matter.

Reproductive health includes accurate information, hygiene, nutrition, and body safety: your body belongs to you, unsafe touch is never the child's fault, and a trusted adult, school counsellor, adolescent health clinic (AFHC) or Childline 1098 can help.

skills.title: Define biodiversity at the levels of species, genes and ecosystems
Explain what a biodiversity hotspot is and why parts of India qualify
Explain why biodiversity matters and how it is threatened and protected

expectations: Biodiversity is the variety of all living things in an area: different species, the genetic variety within species, and the variety of ecosystems.
It includes microbes, fungi, insects, plants and small animals, not just large mammals; most species are small.

A biodiversity hotspot is a region with very many endemic species (found nowhere else) that is also under serious threat. India has parts of four: the Western Ghats, the Himalaya, Indo-Burma (Northeast), and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands).
India has only about 2.4% of the world's land but about 7-8% of recorded species, because of its varied climates and landforms.

Biodiversity gives food, medicine, clean water, pollination, soil fertility and resilience; threats include habitat loss, pollution, invasive species, over-harvesting and climate change; protection includes national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and community efforts.

skills.title: Explain why we classify living things and the basis used (cell type, body organisation, mode of nutrition)
Place organisms in the five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia
Classify tricky cases (fungi, whales, bats) using defining features rather than appearance or habitat

expectations: Classification groups organisms by shared features, making the huge diversity easier to study and showing relationships.
Key bases: prokaryotic or eukaryotic cells, unicellular or multicellular, mode of nutrition (making own food or taking it in), cell wall or not.

Monera: prokaryotes such as bacteria; Protista: unicellular eukaryotes (Amoeba, Paramecium, some algae); Fungi: eukaryotes with chitin cell walls that absorb food from dead or living matter (saprophytes, parasites); Plantae: multicellular, cellulose walls, photosynthesis; Animalia: multicellular, no cell walls, take in food.
Fungi are not plants: they lack chlorophyll and cannot make their own food, and their cell walls are made of chitin.
Defining features, not habitat or looks, decide the group: whales are mammals (lungs, warm blood, feed milk), bats are mammals (fur, milk), not birds.

skills.title: Order the classification hierarchy: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Write and interpret binomial names correctly
Explain fossils as evidence of past life and how they form

expectations: Hierarchy from broadest to narrowest: kingdom → phylum → class → order → family → genus → species; organisms share more features the lower the level.
A species is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
Binomial nomenclature (Linnaeus): genus name with a capital letter + species name in lower case, both in italics (underlined when handwritten), e.g. Panthera tigris, Homo sapiens, Mangifera indica.
Scientific names are precise and the same worldwide, while common names vary by language and region and can refer to different organisms.
Fossils are preserved remains or traces (bones, shells, footprints, impressions) of organisms from long ago, usually formed when remains are quickly buried in sediment that hardens into rock.
Fossils show that life has changed over time; deeper rock layers usually hold older fossils. Dinosaur eggs and bones have been found at Balasinor, Gujarat.

misconceptions.belief: Common names are as precise as scientific names.
signs: Thinks 'jungle cat' or 'bear' names one species everywhere
Ignores regional names

skills.title: Explain that the angle of sunlight, not distance from the Sun, causes uneven heating with latitude
Explain how the Earth's spherical shape and tilted axis cause seasons and different day lengths
Explain how the atmosphere, land and water, and altitude modify heating

expectations: Because the Earth is a sphere, sunlight strikes the equator almost directly and the poles at a low slant; the same beam spreads over a larger area at high latitudes, so each square metre gets less energy.
Slanted rays also pass through more atmosphere, losing more energy before reaching the ground.
The difference in Earth-Sun distance across places on Earth is negligible; in fact the Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter.
The Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so through the year each hemisphere in turn gets more direct sunlight and longer days: this causes seasons.
Land heats and cools faster than water, so coasts have milder temperatures; places at higher altitude are colder because air thins and cools with height.

skills.title: Explain that wind is air moving from high to low pressure caused by uneven heating
Explain sea and land breezes and the Indian monsoon
Explain ocean currents as driven by winds and by differences in temperature and salinity

expectations: Warm air expands, becomes less dense and rises, creating lower pressure; cooler, denser air sinks, creating higher pressure; air flows from high to low pressure as wind.
Sea breeze (day): land heats faster, warm air rises over land, cooler air flows in from the sea. Land breeze (night): land cools faster, so air flows from land to sea.
The monsoon is like a giant seasonal sea breeze: in summer the Indian landmass heats strongly, drawing moist south-west winds from the Indian Ocean, which bring rain; in winter the flow reverses.
The Earth's rotation deflects winds and currents (Coriolis effect): to the right in the northern hemisphere.

Ocean currents are large, steady flows of water driven mainly by winds over the surface and by differences in water temperature and salinity (density); tides cause rise and fall of sea level and local tidal currents, but not the great ocean currents.
Currents carry heat around the planet, warming or cooling coasts, and in the north Indian Ocean they reverse with the monsoon.

misconceptions.belief: Ocean currents are caused only by tides.
signs: Explains the Gulf Stream by the Moon
Thinks currents reverse twice a day
Ignores winds and density

items.prompt_en: What is wind, and what causes it?
items.prompt_hi: Hawa (wind) kya hai, aur iski wajah kya hai?
items.answer: Moving air, flowing from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure; pressure differences come from uneven heating.
acceptable: air from high to low pressure
hints: Air moves from where to where?

items.prompt_en: Why do the south-west monsoon winds bring rain to Kerala in June?
items.prompt_hi: South-west monsoon hawaayein June mein Kerala mein baarish kyon laati hain?
items.answer: In summer the Indian land heats strongly, creating low pressure; moist air from the cooler Indian Ocean (high pressure) flows in; when it rises over the Western Ghats it cools and its water vapour condenses into rain.
acceptable: low pressure over hot land draws moist ocean air

items.prompt_en: Contrast tides and ocean currents.

items.answer: Tides: regular rise and fall of sea level, about twice a day, caused mainly by the Moon's (and Sun's) gravity. Ocean currents: steady large-scale flows of water in fixed directions, driven by winds and differences in temperature and salinity.
acceptable: tides up-down by Moon; currents flows by wind and density

items.answer: The Moon's gravity causes tides. Large ocean currents are driven by winds blowing over the surface and by differences in water temperature and salinity (density).

items.prompt_en: Why does a kite fly well at a beach in the afternoon but the wind direction seems to flip after sunset?

items.answer: In the afternoon the land is warmer, so a sea breeze blows inland; after sunset the land cools faster than the sea, so the pressure difference reverses and a land breeze blows out to sea.

items.prompt_en: Why does the warm Gulf Stream current keep Britain's winters milder than places at the same latitude in Canada?

items.answer: Ocean currents carry heat; the Gulf Stream brings warm tropical water north-east across the Atlantic, warming the air over western Europe.

items.prompt_en: Draw a cross-section diagram of a sea breeze. Label warm land, cool sea, low pressure, high pressure and the direction of air flow at the ground and higher up.
items.prompt_hi: Sea breeze ka cross-section diagram banao. Garam zameen, thanda samudra, low pressure, high pressure aur zameen ke paas aur upar hawa ki disha label karo.
items.answer: Over land: warm air rising (low pressure at the surface). Over sea: cool air sinking (high pressure). At the surface, an arrow from sea to land; higher up, a return arrow from land to sea, completing the loop.

items.prompt_en: Why does very cold, salty water sink near the poles, and how does this drive deep ocean currents?
items.prompt_hi: Dhruvon ke paas bahut thanda, namkeen paani kyon doobta hai, aur isse gehre samudri currents kaise chalte hain?

items.prompt_en: Explain to a friend how the Indian monsoon is like a giant sea breeze.
items.prompt_hi: Ek dost ko samjhao ki Indian monsoon ek bahut bade sea breeze jaisa kaise hai.
items.answer: Key idea: uneven heating of land and sea; summer: land hotter → low pressure over India → moist ocean winds flow in (south-west) → rain when air rises and cools; winter: land cooler → winds reverse (north-east), mostly dry; same mechanism as a daily sea/land breeze but on a seasonal, continental scale.

items.prompt_en: Does wind blow from high pressure to low pressure, or the other way?
items.prompt_hi: Hawa high pressure se low pressure ki taraf chalti hai ya ulta?
items.answer: From high pressure to low pressure.
hints: Like air leaving a pumped tyre

Describe the nitrogen cycle, including fixation by Rhizobium in root nodules
Explain that atoms are recycled, not destroyed, when organisms die

expectations: Matter cycles through living and non-living parts of the Earth; atoms are reused again and again, while energy flows through and is eventually lost as heat.
Water cycle: evaporation from oceans and transpiration from plants → condensation into clouds → precipitation → run-off into rivers and seepage into groundwater.

Carbon cycle: plants take in CO₂ in photosynthesis; respiration by plants, animals and decomposers and burning of fuels return CO₂ to the air; carbon is also stored in fossil fuels, oceans and limestone.
Oxygen cycle: released by photosynthesis, used in respiration and combustion; linked closely to the carbon cycle.

Nitrogen cycle: plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly; nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium in root nodules of pulses, and free-living soil bacteria) and lightning convert it into compounds plants can absorb; animals get nitrogen by eating plants; decomposers return it to the soil; denitrifying bacteria return it to the air.
When organisms die, decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down their bodies and return the atoms to the soil and air for reuse; the atoms are not destroyed.

misconceptions.belief: The atoms in our bodies are destroyed when we die.
signs: Says the body 'disappears' after decay
Does not know what decomposers do
Thinks matter is used up

diagnostic.prompt_en: A fallen leaf decays completely over months. What happens to its carbon and nitrogen atoms?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Gira hua patta mahinon mein poora sad jaata hai. Uske carbon aur nitrogen atoms ka kya hota hai?

options.text: They are destroyed
Decomposers release them as CO₂ into the air and as nitrogen compounds into the soil, to be used again by plants
They stay inside the leaf forever

remediation.representation: Atom-tracking card: one carbon atom's journey from air → leaf → soil → air → another leaf
remediation.moveShape: Child follows one atom through three organisms and says where it is now

misconceptions.belief: Plants take nitrogen directly from the air.
signs: Says plants breathe in nitrogen like oxygen
Does not know why farmers grow pulses in rotation
Thinks fertiliser is unnecessary because air is 78% nitrogen

diagnostic.prompt_en: Air is about 78% nitrogen. Why do farmers still add fertiliser or grow pulses like moong?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Hawa mein lagbhag 78% nitrogen hai. Phir bhi kisaan khaad kyon daalte hain ya moong jaisi daalein kyon ugaate hain?

options.text: They don't need to; plants take nitrogen from the air
Plants cannot use nitrogen gas; it must be fixed into soil compounds by bacteria (like Rhizobium in pulse root nodules), lightning or fertilisers
Pulses absorb nitrogen through their leaves

remediation.representation: Root of a moong plant with pink nodules magnified, showing Rhizobium bacteria
remediation.moveShape: If possible, gently pull a pulse plant from a pot and look for nodules on its roots

items.prompt_en: Name the processes that move water from (a) the sea to the clouds, (b) the clouds to the ground, (c) plant leaves to the air.
items.prompt_hi: Woh processes batao jo paani ko (a) samudra se baadal tak, (b) baadal se zameen tak, (c) patton se hawa tak le jaate hain.
items.answer: (a) evaporation then condensation, (b) precipitation, (c) transpiration.

items.prompt_en: Predict: a dead earthworm is buried in moist soil. After some weeks, what has happened to it, and where are its atoms?
items.prompt_hi: Socho: ek mara hua kenchua geeli mitti mein dabaaya. Kuch hafton baad uska kya hua, aur uske atoms kahan hain?
items.answer: Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) have broken it down; its carbon has largely returned to the air as CO₂ and its nitrogen and minerals to the soil, ready for plants.
acceptable: decomposed; atoms in soil and air

items.prompt_en: Predict: a field grows wheat three years in a row versus a field that alternates wheat with moong. Which needs more nitrogen fertiliser, and why?
items.prompt_hi: Socho: ek khet mein teen saal lagaatar gehun, aur doosre mein gehun aur moong baari-baari. Kisko zyada nitrogen khaad chahiye, aur kyon?
items.answer: The wheat-only field: wheat removes nitrogen from soil; moong (a legume) has Rhizobium in its root nodules that fixes nitrogen, restoring the soil.
hints: What do the bacteria in nodules do?
Wheat-only needs more; pulses fix nitrogen

items.prompt_en: Contrast photosynthesis and respiration in their roles in the carbon cycle.
items.prompt_hi: Carbon cycle mein photosynthesis aur respiration ki bhoomika ka fark batao.
items.answer: Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air and builds it into sugars, releasing O₂; respiration breaks sugars down, using O₂ and returning CO₂ to the air.
acceptable: photosynthesis takes CO2, respiration releases CO2

items.prompt_en: Why can't most plants use the nitrogen gas that makes up 78% of air?
items.prompt_hi: Hawa ka 78% nitrogen hai, phir bhi zyaadatar paudhe use use kyon nahi kar sakte?
items.answer: The two nitrogen atoms in N₂ are held by a very strong triple bond; plants cannot break it, so they depend on nitrogen-fixing bacteria or lightning to convert it into nitrates and ammonium they can absorb through roots.
hints: How strong is the N≡N bond?
Bond too strong; bacteria fix it

items.prompt_en: A student writes, 'When animals die, their bodies are destroyed and the matter is gone.' Correct it.
items.prompt_hi: Ek student likhta hai, 'Jaanwar marte hain toh unka sharir nasht ho jaata hai aur matter khatam.' Theek karo.
items.answer: The body decomposes; decomposers return its carbon, nitrogen and minerals to the soil, water and air, where plants and other organisms reuse them. Matter is recycled, not destroyed.

items.prompt_en: Why do the leaves of a potted plant covered with a clear plastic bag show water droplets inside the bag after a few hours?
items.prompt_hi: Gamle ke paudhe ko clear plastic bag se dhak do toh kuch ghanton mein bag ke andar paani ki boondein kyon dikhti hain?
items.answer: Transpiration: the plant releases water vapour from its leaves, which condenses on the cooler bag surface.
hints: Where did the water come from?

items.prompt_en: How does cutting large areas of forest affect the carbon cycle and the amount of CO₂ in the air?
items.prompt_hi: Bade jungal kaatne se carbon cycle aur hawa mein CO₂ ki maatra pe kya asar padta hai?
items.answer: Fewer trees take in CO₂ by photosynthesis, and burning or rotting the cut wood releases stored carbon, so CO₂ in the air rises, adding to global warming.
acceptable: less absorption, more release, CO2 rises
hints: What happens to the carbon in cut trees?

items.prompt_en: Draw a cycle diagram for nitrogen with these boxes: air (N₂), root nodules, soil nitrates, plants, animals, decomposers.
items.prompt_hi: Nitrogen ka cycle diagram in boxes se banao: hawa (N₂), root nodules, mitti ke nitrates, paudhe, jaanwar, decomposers.
items.answer: Air N₂ → (fixation by Rhizobium in root nodules, lightning) → soil nitrates → absorbed by plants → eaten by animals → wastes and dead bodies → decomposers → ammonia/nitrates in soil → denitrifying bacteria → back to air N₂.
hints: How does N₂ enter the soil?
How does it return to air?

items.prompt_en: Why is the water cycle important for life on land?
items.prompt_hi: Zameen pe jeevan ke liye water cycle kyon zaroori hai?
items.answer: It continually moves fresh water from oceans to land as rain, refilling rivers, lakes and groundwater that plants, animals and people need; evaporation also leaves salt behind, so rain is fresh.
hints: Where does rain water come from?
Fresh water to land, again and again

items.prompt_en: Tell the story of one carbon atom that was once in a dinosaur and is now in you.
items.prompt_hi: Ek carbon atom ki kahaani sunaao jo kabhi dinosaur mein tha aur ab tumhare andar hai.
items.answer: Key idea: atoms are recycled; the dinosaur's carbon returned to the air as CO₂ via respiration or decomposition; plants fixed it by photosynthesis; it passed through food chains, oceans or rocks over millions of years; you ate a plant (or animal) containing it; atoms are not destroyed.
hints: How did carbon leave the dinosaur?
Who takes CO₂ from the air?

items.prompt_en: Which bacteria live in the root nodules of pulses, and what do they do?
items.prompt_hi: Daalon ki jadon ke nodules mein kaunse bacteria rehte hain, aur kya karte hain?
items.answer: Rhizobium; they fix atmospheric nitrogen into compounds the plant can use.
hints: They turn N₂ into usable compounds

workedExample.problem: Trace one nitrogen atom from the air to a person eating dal and back to the air.
steps: Rhizobium bacteria in the root nodules of a moong plant fix N₂ from the air into ammonium compounds
The plant uses them to build proteins in its seeds (the moong dal)
A person eats the dal; the nitrogen becomes part of their proteins
Wastes (urea) and, eventually, dead bodies are broken down by decomposers into ammonia and nitrates in soil
Denitrifying bacteria convert some nitrates back into N₂, returning the atom to the air
fadedVersion: ___ break down wastes into soil nitrogen
Denitrifying bacteria return it to the ___

skills.title: Distinguish weather from climate
Explain how human activities (burning fuels, deforestation, stubble burning, fertiliser run-off) disrupt natural cycles
Explain the enhanced greenhouse effect and its consequences
Evaluate responses at personal, community and policy levels

expectations: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere (today's temperature, rain, wind); climate is the average pattern over decades (about 30 years) in a region.
Burning fossil fuels and forests adds CO₂ faster than plants and oceans can absorb it; the enhanced greenhouse effect traps more heat, raising global average temperature.
Consequences include more heatwaves, changing monsoon patterns and heavy rain events, glacier melt, sea-level rise and stress on crops and health.
Stubble burning in north India releases smoke particles and gases; in winter cool, still air traps them near the ground, causing severe smog over the plains.
Excess fertiliser washed into lakes causes algal blooms and oxygen loss (eutrophication); deforestation disturbs the water and carbon cycles.

Responses: cleaner energy (solar), efficient transport, tree planting and forest protection, alternatives to stubble burning (machines like the Happy Seeder, decomposer sprays), careful fertiliser use, and personal habits (saving electricity, less waste).

misconceptions.belief: Climate and weather are the same thing.
signs: Says 'it's cold today, so global warming is fake'
Uses one rainy week as proof of climate change
Cannot say over what time climate is measured

diagnostic.prompt_en: Delhi has an unusually cold week in January. Does this disprove global warming?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Delhi mein January mein ek hafta bahut thanda raha. Kya isse global warming galat sabit hoti hai?

options.text: Yes, if it's cold, the planet isn't warming
No; one week is weather. Climate change is about long-term averages over decades across the globe
Yes, because climate means the temperature today

remediation.representation: A noisy temperature line over 100 years with a clear upward trend line drawn through it
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child to point to one cold dip and then to the trend; which one is climate?

misconceptions.belief: The greenhouse effect is entirely bad and is the same as the ozone hole.
signs: Says we should remove all greenhouse gases
Mixes up ozone depletion and warming
Does not know Earth would be frozen without it

diagnostic.prompt_en: Without any natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average temperature would be:
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Agar koi bhi natural greenhouse effect na ho, toh Earth ka average temperature kya hoga?

options.text: The same as now
Around −18 °C, far too cold for most life; the problem today is the extra (enhanced) effect from human emissions
Much hotter

remediation.representation: Blanket analogy: one blanket keeps you comfortable; piling on more makes you overheat
remediation.moveShape: Ask what happens with no blanket and with five blankets

items.prompt_en: Classify as weather or climate: (a) 'It will rain in Pune tomorrow.' (b) 'Rajasthan gets little rain most years.' (c) 'Kerala's average June rainfall is high.'
items.prompt_hi: Weather ya climate batao: (a) 'Kal Pune mein baarish hogi.' (b) 'Rajasthan mein zyaadatar saal kam baarish hoti hai.' (c) 'Kerala mein June ki average baarish zyada hai.'
items.answer: (a) weather, (b) climate, (c) climate.

items.prompt_en: Predict: why is Delhi's smog usually worst in November-December rather than in June?
items.prompt_hi: Socho: Delhi ka smog aam taur pe June ki jagah November-December mein sabse bura kyon hota hai?
items.answer: Stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana peaks around October-November; in winter, cool, still air near the ground (temperature inversion) and slow winds trap smoke and dust, while firecrackers and vehicles add more. In June, heat and winds lift and spread pollutants, and the monsoon later washes them out.
acceptable: stubble burning plus still cold air traps smoke

items.prompt_en: Predict: if global average temperature keeps rising, what happens to Himalayan glaciers and to rivers like the Ganga over the coming decades?
items.prompt_hi: Socho: agar global average temperature badhta raha, toh aane wale dashakon mein Himalayan glaciers aur Ganga jaisi nadiyon ka kya hoga?
items.answer: Glaciers shrink; rivers may first carry more meltwater and flood risk rises, but in the long run summer flow from melt could fall, affecting water supply and farming.
acceptable: glaciers shrink; flow changes, long-term less meltwater
hints: What does heat do to ice?
Where does river water come from in summer?

items.prompt_en: How does adding CO₂ to the air warm the planet?
items.prompt_hi: Hawa mein CO₂ badhaane se planet garam kaise hota hai?
items.answer: Sunlight warms the Earth's surface, which gives off heat as infrared radiation; CO₂ and other greenhouse gases absorb some of it and send it back down, so more heat stays near the surface. More CO₂ traps more heat.
hints: What does the warm ground give off?
What does CO₂ do to that heat?

items.prompt_en: Compare two ways of dealing with stubble: burning it, and using a Happy Seeder machine or decomposer spray.
items.prompt_hi: Parali se nipatne ke do tareekon ko compare karo: jalaana, aur Happy Seeder machine ya decomposer spray.
items.answer: Burning is quick and cheap for the farmer but causes smog, health damage and loss of soil nutrients and organisms. Happy Seeder sows wheat through the stubble, and decomposer sprays break it down in the field; both avoid smoke and return organic matter to soil, but need equipment, cost or time.
acceptable: burning pollutes; alternatives return matter to soil

items.prompt_en: A post says, 'It snowed heavily in Shimla this year, so climate change is a myth.' What is the error?
items.prompt_hi: Ek post kehti hai, 'Is saal Shimla mein bhaari barf giri, isliye climate change ek myth hai.' Galti kya hai?
items.answer: It confuses weather with climate. A single season in one place is weather; climate change refers to long-term global averages, which are rising. Warming can even bring more extreme events, including heavy snowfall in some years.
hints: Is one season a long-term average?

items.prompt_en: A lake near a farming village turns green and smelly, and fish die. What might have happened?
items.prompt_hi: Ek khet waale gaon ke paas ki jheel hari aur badboodar ho gayi, aur machhliyaan mar gayin. Kya hua hoga?
items.answer: Excess fertiliser washed into the lake fed a huge growth of algae (algal bloom); when the algae died, decomposers used up the dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocated (eutrophication).
acceptable: fertiliser run-off caused algal bloom and oxygen loss

items.prompt_en: Your school wants to cut its carbon footprint. Suggest three practical actions and explain which natural cycle each helps.
items.prompt_hi: Tumhara school apna carbon footprint kam karna chahta hai. Teen practical kadam suggest karo aur batao har ek kis natural cycle ki madad karta hai.
items.answer: Examples: rooftop solar panels (less fossil fuel burning, carbon cycle); planting and caring for native trees (more CO₂ absorbed, carbon and water cycles); composting canteen food waste instead of dumping or burning it (returns nutrients to soil, carbon and nitrogen cycles); switching off fans and lights (less electricity).

items.prompt_en: A graph shows CO₂ in air rising from about 315 ppm in 1960 to about 420 ppm in 2024, with a small up-down wiggle each year. Describe the trend and explain the wiggle.
items.prompt_hi: Ek graph mein hawa ka CO₂ 1960 mein lagbhag 315 ppm se 2024 mein lagbhag 420 ppm tak badhta hai, har saal ek chhoti upar-neeche lehar ke saath. Trend batao aur lehar samjhao.
items.answer: A steady long-term rise due to burning fossil fuels and deforestation. The yearly wiggle is from northern hemisphere plants: CO₂ dips in summer when they photosynthesise more and rises in winter when they lose leaves and decay.
acceptable: rising trend; seasonal wiggle from plant growth

items.prompt_en: Why does cutting forests in a hilly area lead to more floods and landslides during heavy rain?
items.prompt_hi: Pahaadi ilaake mein jungle kaatne se tez baarish mein baadh aur landslides zyada kyon hote hain?
items.answer: Tree roots bind soil and forests slow rainwater, letting it soak in; without them water runs off quickly carrying soil, so rivers rise faster and slopes become unstable. The water cycle's balance between infiltration and run-off is disturbed.
acceptable: less soaking, more run-off, loose soil
hints: What do roots do to soil?
Where does rain go without trees?

items.prompt_en: Explain to your family the difference between the natural greenhouse effect and global warming, and one thing your home could do.
items.prompt_hi: Apne parivaar ko natural greenhouse effect aur global warming ka fark samjhao, aur ek cheez jo ghar pe kar sakte ho.
items.answer: Key idea: natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable (~15 °C instead of −18 °C); burning fuels adds extra CO₂ → enhanced effect → warming; weather ≠ climate; home action: save electricity, LED bulbs, public transport, less waste, solar water heater.
hints: What would Earth be like with no greenhouse gases?
Natural blanket vs extra blankets; save energy

items.prompt_en: Over roughly how many years is climate averaged?
items.prompt_hi: Climate ka average lagbhag kitne saalon mein nikaala jaata hai?
items.answer: About 30 years (decades).

workedExample.problem: Explain how stubble burning in Punjab leads to smog in Delhi, and suggest a response.
steps: After the rice harvest, farmers burn leftover stubble to clear fields quickly for wheat
Burning releases smoke particles, carbon monoxide and CO₂ (the carbon cycle is pushed towards the air), and soil nutrients are lost
North-westerly winds carry the smoke towards Delhi
In winter, cool still air near the ground does not rise, trapping smoke with vehicle and dust pollution: smog
Response: Happy Seeder machines, decomposer sprays, using stubble as fodder or fuel pellets, with support for farmers
fadedVersion: Cold still air ___ the smoke: smog
